items.title: Nobody called it the Wars of the Roses at the time
items.claim: The wars between Lancaster and York (1455-1487) are remembered for the red and white rose badges. What is the actual history of those symbols?

options.text: Both sides wore rose badges throughout the conflict
The white rose was a Yorkist badge, but the red Lancastrian rose was largely a Tudor-era invention — Henry VII used the union of the roses as propaganda
The roses came from heraldic tradition dating to the Conquest
The name was coined in 1485 by Henry VII himself

items.reveal_title: The Tudor rose was the spin
items.reveal:
Edward IV used a white rose among other badges. The red rose was a minor Lancastrian badge under Henry IV but rarely used during the wars themselves. The 'Tudor rose' (red and white combined) was created after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486 — the union as legitimising symbol.

The name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularised by Walter Scott's novel 'Anne of Geierstein' (1829). Shakespeare's 'Henry VI Part 1' invented the Temple Garden scene where nobles pluck the rival roses.
items.why: Historical memory is shaped by later spin. The Tudor regime had every reason to dramatise dynastic union; Shakespeare amplified the imagery; Scott named it. Almost none of that was visible in 1460.

items.title: Henry VII was a 'modern' monarch — by destroying the nobility
items.claim: How did Henry VII (r. 1485-1509) consolidate power?

options.text: By distributing land widely among loyal nobles
By using bonds and recognisances to financially bind nobles, the Star Chamber to bypass juries, and avoiding war to keep crown finances strong
By creating a standing army of 50,000 men
By moving the capital from London to York

items.reveal:
Henry VII forced nobles to enter bonds — written debts payable to the crown on bad behaviour. By 1509 around two-thirds of the peerage was under bond. Empson and Dudley managed crown revenue ruthlessly.

The Star Chamber, sitting at Westminster, dealt with cases the common-law courts could not — overmighty nobles intimidating juries. Henry VII left £1.5 million in the treasury (his son spent it in a decade). He fought one continental war.
items.why: Henry VII is the boring Tudor — but his fiscal-administrative state is what makes Henry VIII's ambition possible. Modern bureaucratic monarchy starts here, not at the Reformation.
